final.memo:
GEICO is an automobile insurer that bypassed the traditional commissioned agent system to offer low-cost coverage to consumers [D01]. We have long understood the economics of this business, which relies on a permanent structural expense advantage rather than the expensive distribution networks used by most competitors [D01].

Historically, this expense advantage resulted in superior returns and market share growth, even if recent years have been marred by a catastrophic breakdown in underwriting discipline [D02, D06]. While the combined ratio of 124.2% in 1975 indicates a severe loss of control, the underlying low-cost model remains a potent weapon if properly managed [D01, D02].

In May 1976, the company appointed Jack Byrne as CEO to lead a massive rehabilitation [D03, D07]. We trust that an owner-minded manager with a clear mandate for underwriting discipline and rate adequacy can restore the profitability that this franchise previously demonstrated [D03].

The market has largely priced the company for extinction, fearing imminent regulatory seizure due to a premium-to-surplus ratio of 13.40:1 [D05, D06]. We believe this pessimism ignores the resiliency of the direct-to-consumer model and the ability of the company to shed poor-quality risks under new leadership [D01, D05].

At a market price of $3.50, we are buying a stake in a recovery that, if successful, will be worth substantially more than the current $2.08 book value [D04]. While we lack a positive earnings yield today, the alternative of holding long bonds at 7.88% is less attractive than deploying capital into a distressed situation where our intervention can aid a structural turnaround [D04, D08].

The risks here are binary: we face the potential for a permanent loss of capital if regulators conclude that the reserve deficiency cannot be bridged [D05]. However, the scale of the potential recovery and the soundness of the core insurance model justify an initial allocation of 10% of our partnership assets to support this turnaround [D08].
